newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire fighting sparks refugee exodus.
newsitem.headline: Zaire fighting sparks refugee exodus.

text.p: Hoards of Hutu refugees from Rwanda and Burundi were on the move in eastern Zaire on Monday in search of a safe haven from fighting between soldiers and ethnic Tutsi rebels there, humanitarian sources said.

The exodus coincided with reports from the U.N. refugee agency in Geneva and humanitarian sources in the region that fighting had spread from South Kivu near the border with Burundi to North Kivu and the region of Goma bordering Rwanda.
In London, Zairean Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo expressed concern about events and said neighbouring Rwanda threatened to be "a detonator for an explosion" in the sub-region.
"Unfortunately that's what it's doing," he added in remarks broadcast by the British Broadcasting Corporation.

Estimates of the size of the exodus from 12 refugee camps near Uvira by the border with Burundi ranged up to a quarter of a million. Some sources said they had taken to nearby mountains, others that they were heading for Bukavu.
There was no reliable status report on the fighting or death toll -- apart from 28 civilians killed near Uvira on Friday and a Zairean soldier reported killed near Goma on Sunday.

But with Zaire reinforcing and resupplying its troops in the eastern refugee zone, U.N. Under Secretary General Ibrahima Fall held urgent talks in the South Kivu regional capital of Bukavu in an attempt to calm passions and defuse tension.

"I will report to the (U.N.) secretary-general (Boutros Boutros-Ghali) so that he can inform the Security Council," Fall, who arrived on Sunday, told Reuters. "I am sure that the Security Council will take up its responsibilities."

In Addis Ababa, the Organisation of African Unity said it was sending an envoy to assess the exodus. "The OAU follows with grave concern the unfolding tragic events in the countries of the Great Lakes region which has caused the exodus of thousands of refugees," it added.
Fighting between Banyamulenge, Tutsis who came to Zaire late in the 18th century, and troops follows Banyamulenge accusations that indigenous Zaireans are trying to force them out.

It has fuelled fears that the Tutsi and Hutu hatred and rivalry which triggered the 1994 genocide of almost a million Tutsis in Rwanda and the equally bitter civil war in Burundi could engulf the whole Central African Great Lakes region.
Zaire, host to over a million Hutus who fled Rwanda and Burundi fearing reprisals from Tutsi-dominated armies, accuses Rwanda of sending Banyamulenge to destabilise the refugee zone.
Rwanda's Tutsi-dominated government says Hutu hardliners use Zaire as a launchpad for attacks on Rwandan territory.
A Zairean officer at Nyaneezi army camp about 30 km south of Bukavu said military operations continued on Monday. Traders spoke of sporadic fighting in areas to which they had access.

Paul Stromberg, spokesman for the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees in Rwanda, said in Kigali some 221,000 refugees were heading for towards Bukavu. "There is continuing fighting around Bwegera, midway between Uvira and Bukavu," he added.
Humanitarian sources in Bukavu said that refugee camps around Uvira had emptied but it unclear whether the refugees were headed for Bukavu.

Rwanda on Monday denied any link with the fighting after aid sources reported unidentified fighters crossing from Rwanda and attacking army positions in Zaire. "We are not involved in operations in north or south Kivu," army spokesman Major Wilson Rutayisire said. "We are not arming the Banyamulenge."
